title: 2026 budget review and tax increase debate
subtitle: Waste collection changes, user fees, water rates, housing capital delays, airport, roads, and GRCA budget presentation
overview: The Strategic Planning and Budget Committee spent two days reviewing the Region's preliminary 2026 plan, operating budget and capital program. It received the preliminary plan and the 2026 user fees and charges for information. Staff presented a budget at about a 5% tax guideline, with the operating side covering waste, transit, user fees and water and wastewater rates.

The main vote came on whether staff should return on December 3 with options for a lower property tax increase. The committee defeated a proposal for 2.2% {{vote:m1}} and a proposal for 3% {{vote:m2}}. Staff said any extra reductions would have to be prepared within a week, without the usual review. Final budget decisions remain with Council in December.

Residents will see changes to garbage and bulky item collection starting in March 2026, and higher landfill and some other fees. The committee also heard that some regional housing projects, including Moorgate, may be delayed because of debt limits. The committee asked staff for many follow-up reports for December 3. It also heard a presentation on the Grand River Conservation Authority's 2026 budget, which it received for information.
The committee also went into closed session on staff compensation labour relations, and a later closed Council meeting was scheduled for November 19.

decisions.detail: The committee defeated a request that staff bring options on December 3 to reach a 2026 operating budget, excluding Police Services, with a 2.2% property tax increase {{vote:m1}}.
The committee defeated a request that staff bring options on December 3 to reach a 2026 operating budget, excluding Police Services, with a 3% property tax increase {{vote:m2}}.

debate: Supporters of a lower tax target said affordability is a serious concern for residents on fixed incomes. They said the Region's five-year average increase was well above Ontario inflation. They said asking for options would inform Council without binding it to adopt them.

Opponents said the request came too late, since a 5% target was set in June, and that staff would have only about a week without normal vetting. Staff said a 3% target would need roughly $8 million to $11.6 million more in adjustments, and 2.2% would need further reductions of about $16 million. Staff also said a longer list of higher-risk items would have to be made public.

Several councillors warned that further cuts could hit services people rely on, such as transit, food security supports, downtown garbage collection and legislated services. One councillor said a 2.2% increase would still be about $43 per average household, against about $96 at the proposed level.

On waste, councillors raised concern about confusion between Region and Circular Materials collection, the loss of double-up days, cart swap delays, and the Sanican (downtown litter bin) removal. Staff agreed to report on the Sanican question, bulky item options, and a shared calendar on December 3.

On housing, councillors worried that deferring Moorgate could put CMHC funding at risk. Staff said debt servicing could reach about 21% of the housing and homelessness budget, and that partnership options and a possible housing levy were being explored.
